query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Grain boundary decohesion in high-entropy alloys can lead to brittle behavior due to localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries, even in the absence of significant grain boundary segregation and phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy with a compositionally complex solid solution structure
generation.intervention: High strain rate shear or sliding contact
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary energy and grain boundary sliding mechanisms
generation.mechanism: Dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall-Petch behavior in the surface layer, leading to grain boundary decohesion
generation.predicted_outcome: Emergence of brittle behavior, characterized by low ductility and high susceptibility to fracture
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with grain boundary segregation and phase separation
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 400° to 800°C, where single-phase fcc high- and medium-entropy alloys exhibit a rapid decrease in ductility
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of grain boundary decohesion in high-entropy alloys and its relationship to the alloy's composition and microstructure

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of high-entropy alloys with different grain boundary energies and sliding contact conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy exhibits no significant grain boundary decohesion or brittle behavior under high strain rate shear or sliding contact, the hypothesis is falsified.

Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,].
